data.text:
Remarks of the Deputy Spokesperson of the Chinese Embassy Guo Wei in Response to Jay Tarriela’s Flawed Argument about the Bilateral Trade Relations

Q: In a social media post, Jay Tarriela downplayed the trade relations between the Philippines and China, citing sources from the Stratbase Institute. “Official (Philippine) government data show that China's contribution to Philippine investment inflows is limited, while trade relations remain structurally imbalanced.” What is your comment?

A: Mr. Jay Tarriela’s argument contains several logical and analytical flaws that weaken its credibility. He is misleading the public about the true scope of engagement between China and the Philippines.

First, he reflects overgeneralization through selective framing. China–Philippines economic cooperation is multidimensional. It encompasses trade in goods and services, two-way investment flows, industrial, infrastructure and development cooperation etc. When one isolates only investment as the sole indicators of the relationship’s value, the analysis becomes structurally incomplete. 

Second, he mischaracterizes established economic facts. China has been the Philippines’ largest trading partner for nine consecutive years, which by definition indicates sustained and systemic economic interaction. In 2025, China (including Hong Kong and Macao) supplied US$40.1 billion in imports to the Philippines and purchased US$21.6 billion in Philippine exports. This scale of two-way trade supports production networks, stabilizes consumer prices, and sustains export-oriented sectors.

Moreover, economic cooperation has extended beyond commerce. During the COVID-19 pandemic, China provided more than 55 million vaccine doses, contributing to public health stabilization and economic reopening. In parallel, development cooperation has produced tangible infrastructure outcomes, including the Binondo–Intramuros Bridge, the Estrella–Pantaleon Bridge, the Davao River (Bucana) Bridge, the Chico River Pump Irrigation Project, and the Samal Island–Davao City Connector Project. These projects reduce congestion, improve connectivity, and enhance long-term productivity. 

Humanitarian assistance has also been concrete and measurable: 10,000 tons of rice after Super Typhoon Rai in 2021; irrigation support for 8,700 hectares of farmland in 2022; 20,000 tons of fertilizer in 2023; and in November 2025, US$1 million in cash assistance plus RMB 10 million worth of relief supplies following multiple natural disasters. 

Third, even if focusing narrowly on trade, proper context is essential. Trade balances are shaped primarily by market forces and structural differences between economies, not by deliberate pursuit of surplus. In 2025, China absorbed 25.6 percent of total Philippine exports (US$21.6 billion), exceeding its exports to the United States (US$13.4 billion) and Japan (US$11.6 billion). China is also a major market for durian, pineapple, and banana exports, sustaining livelihoods across rural provinces. At the China International Import Expo, three Davao durian exporters secured US$36.6 million in deals last year, demonstrating concrete market access. 

Furthermore, any evaluation that excludes services trade is analytically incomplete. In 2019, 1.74 million Chinese tourists visited the Philippines, spending over US$2.3 billion and supporting thousands of jobs. At the same time, approximately half a million Filipinos working in China generate remittances that reinforce household income and domestic consumption. 

Fourth, even if discussing investment, it requires methodological caution and avoidance of survivorship bias. Investment flows fluctuate due to global cycles, regulatory environments, and geopolitical dynamics. After the pandemic, during President Marcos’s January 2023 state visit to China, investment pledges totaling US$22.8 billion were announced. At the moment, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority, Chinese companies pledged ₱10.25 billion in 2025, more than triple the ₱2.43 billion recorded the previous year. Meanwhile, member firms of the Chinese Enterprises Philippine Association (CEPA) report more than 150,000 direct jobs created with Chinese investment. In synergy with trade and government-to-government cooperation projects, it has supported millions of jobs along related industrial chains. 

Last but not least, a serious discussion must address underlying causes rather than rhetorical impressions. Jay Tarriela appears notably unconcerned about the practical welfare implications for ordinary Filipinos. It is always easier to gamble with other people’s livelihoods when your own paycheck is not on the table. However, the key question is: setting aside the COVID-19 disruptions of 2019–2022, why have Chinese investment and trade with the Philippines fallen since 2023?
